blocks.x: INTRODUCTION:

Guava (Psidium guajava L.), the “poor man’s fruit” or “apple of the tropics” is a popular tree fruit of the tropical and subtropical climate and is native to the tropical America belonging to the family Myrtaceae, Guava occupies fifth place in area and fourth in fruit production in India. In India, it flourishes up to an altitude of 1000 m but the best quality guava is produced in Indo-Gangetic plains. All the cultivars of Indian guava belong to a single species Psidium guajava. About 160 guava cultivars are available in India. In guava, most of the commercial varieties are reported to be diploids, the chromosome number being 2n = 22, except the seedless types which are triploids (Kumar and Ranade, 1952). In India, guava is grown almost in all the states due to its broad adaptability, hardy nature, and ability to thrive under diverse soil and climatic conditions. Bihar has the largest area (24.7 thousand ha.) under guava cultivation followed by Uttar Pradesh (18.5 thousand ha.) and Maharashtra (14.8 thousand ha.). Productivity is the highest in M.P. (20t/ha) very low in U.P. (7.3 t/ha). It is valued for its precocious bearing habit, high productivity, regular cropping, and excellent nutritional quality, being a rich source of vitamin C (150-200 mg/100 g of pulp), pectin, antioxidants, minerals, and dietary fiber. Guava bears fruits almost round-the year. However, two distinct seasons of flowering- April-May and August-September occur from which fruits ripen during rainy and winter season, respectively (Mitra and Sanyal, 2004). Owing to its profitability, resilience, and scope for sustainable intensification, guava plays a vital role in nutritional security, livelihood generation, and horticultural diversification in India. There are number of pathogens, mainly fungal, which affect guava crop besides few bacterial, algal and some physiological disorders or deficiencies. About 177 pathogens are reported on various parts of guava plant of which, 167 are fungal, 3 bacterial, 3 algal, 3 nematodes and one epiphyte. About 91 pathogens are reported on fruits, 42 on foliage, 18 on twig, 18 on root and 17 fungi are isolated from surface of fruits. These pathogens cause various diseases viz. pre and post-harvest rots of fruits (dry rots, wet rots, soft rots, sour rots, anthracnose, brown rots, ripe rots, scab, styler end rots, ring rots, pink rots, waxy fruit rots, etc.), canker, wilt, die back, defoliation, twig drying, leaf spot, leaf blight, anthracnose, red rust, sooty mould, rust, seedling blight, damping off, etc. (Misra and Prakash, 1990).

Effective management of guava diseases depends on an integrated approach involving disease-free planting material, resistant cultivars, sound cultural practices, and timely chemical and biological control measures. A clear understanding of disease symptoms, spread, and epidemiology is essential for sustainable guava production.
WILT:

India, wilt of guava was first reported in 1935 from Babakkarpur (Allahabad). Wilt disease is a major limiting factor for the productivity and production of guava. Since, the disease is soil borne annual yield losses of 5- 15% were reported in Uttar Pradesh (Singh and Lal, 1953), while in West Bengal, yield reduction reached up to 80% in severely affected orchards (Chattopadhyay and Sen Gupta, 1955). Large-scale orchard declines and failure of replanting in wilt-affected soils were also documented (Chattopadhyay and Bhattacharjya, 1968a). In Andhra Pradesh, guava wilt significantly reduced orchard productivity and land value, and extensive orchard removal was reported in Punjab and Haryana due to severe wilt incidence (Jhooty et al., 1984). Later studies around Lucknow recorded yield losses ranging from 5-60%, with plants older than five years showing greater susceptibility (Misra and Shukla, 2002).
Symptoms:

Guava wilt initially appears as chlorosis and slight curling of leaves on terminal branches. Infected plants exhibit browning, drooping, and premature abscission of leaves. Twigs gradually become leafless, fail to produce new shoots or flowers, and dry up. Disease symptoms commonly develop after the rainy season during October-November. Fruits on affected branches remain underdeveloped, hard, stony, and may turn dark brown or black. Roots show black streaking, basal rotting, and easy separation of bark from the cortex. (Das Gupta and Rai, 1947). Vascular and cortical tissues exhibit light brown discoloration due to pathogen invasion. (Chattopadhyaya and Bhattacharjee, 1968a,b). Mainly two symptoms are identified: (a) Slow wilt and (b) Sudden wilt (Chakraborty and Singh, 1989). Severe infection leads to complete defoliation and death of the tree, especially in plants older than ten years.
Fig 1: Wilt infected tree Fig 2: Vascular discoloration
Causal organism:

Guava wilt is a complex disease associated with several pathogens, mainly Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. psidii, Fusarium solani, Macrophomina phaseolina, Rhizoctonia bataticola, Cephalosporium, and Gliocladium roseum, acting singly or synergistically in wilt development (Vestal, 1941; Prasad et al., 1952; Misra and

Pandey, 1997, 2000a). In addition, plant-parasitic nematodes such as Meloidogyne, Helicotylenchus and Pratylenchus have been reported in association with guava wilt and may predispose roots to fungal invasion by causing wounds and weakening root systems (Rodriguez and Landa, 1977).
Disease cycle:
Primary Spread:
Soil and rhizoplane inoculum: Pathogens survive in soil, root debris, and on the rhizoplane, serving as the primary source of infection (Dwivedi, 1991a).
Root penetration: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. psidii enters through the piliferous layer (root hair zone) or openings formed by secondary roots (Edward, 1960b).
Xylem infection: Fusarium solani invades and blocks the xylem vessels, restricting water movement (Chattopadhyay and Bhattacharjya, 1968a,b).
Phloem infection: Macrophomina phaseolina primarily colonizes the phloem, later extending into xylem tissues (Chattopadhyay and Sengupta, 1955).
Petiole infection: Gloeosporium psidii penetrates through the petiole, infecting young leaves and shoots (Tandon and Agarwal, 1954).
Nematode-assisted infection: Root injury caused by Meloidogyne, Helicotylenchus, and Pratylenchus facilitates entry of fungal pathogens into root tissues (Rodriguez and Landa, 1977).
Secondary Spread:
Vascular persistence: Pathogens remain in infected xylem, phloem, roots, and petiole tissues, serving as secondary inoculum (Edward, 1960c; Pandey and Dwivedi, 1985).

Soil movement: Spread occurs through contaminated soil, irrigation water, infected nursery stock, and root-to-root contact (Dwivedi, 1991a). Debris decomposition: Infected roots, stems, petioles, and root residues decompose, releasing inoculum back into soil for subsequent infections (Misra and Pandey, 2000a).
Nematode dissemination: Soil-borne nematodes move through the root zone, causing fresh wounds and enhancing secondary spread of wilt pathogens (Rodriguez and Landa, 1977).
Epidemiology:

The epidemiology of guava wilt is strongly influenced by soil moisture, soil reaction, nutrient status, soil type, and prevailing climatic conditions, which collectively determine disease incidence and severity. Disease development is favoured under moderately high soil moisture, with maximum severity occurring at 40–60% soil saturation when Fusarium solani or Macrophomina phaseolina act individually, whereas 60-80% soil saturation is reported optimum when both pathogens occur in association (Chattopadhyay and Bhattacharjya, 1968b).

Soil reaction markedly affects wilt incidence, with pH 6.0 considered optimum for disease development, while disease intensity declines significantly under strongly acidic (pH 4.0) or alkaline (pH 8.0) conditions (Chattopadhyay and Bhattacharjya, 1968b). However, earlier observations indicated severe wilt incidence in alkaline soils (pH 7.5-9.0) (Mehta, 1951), whereas high disease prevalence was also recorded in lateritic soils with pH 6.5, suggesting that the influence of soil pH may vary depending on soil type, pathogen complex, and edaphic interactions (Sen and Verma, 1954).

Nutritional status of soil also plays a critical role in disease expression. Wilt incidence is comparatively lower at 630 ppm nitrogen, whereas both deficient and excessive nitrogen levels enhance disease susceptibility. Similarly, moderate to high phosphate concentrations (207-345 ppm) significantly suppress wilt development. Incorporation of organic manures into infested soils reduces disease severity, while green manuring has been reported to completely suppress wilt incidence, possibly through improvement of soil microbial antagonism and physicochemical properties (Chattopadhyay and Bhattacharjya, 1968b).

Soil texture further influences disease occurrence, with clay loam and sandy loam soils being more conducive to wilt development than other soil types (Mehta, 1987). Seasonal incidence of guava wilt is closely associated with monsoonal climatic conditions. Disease initiation generally begins with the onset of rains in June-August, followed by rapid intensification during the monsoon period. Maximum plant mortality is consistently recorded during September-October, after which disease incidence gradually declines with the onset of winter (Das Gupta and Rai, 1947; Edward, 1960c; Suhag, 1976).

Weather analysis has shown that high rainfall during July–September, maximum temperature of 31.3-33.5°C, minimum temperature of 23-25°C, and relative humidity around 76% create highly favorable conditions for pathogen growth, infection, and wilt expression (Misra and Pandey, 1999a,d; Misra and Pandey, 2000b). Under such favorable conditions, complete wilting of infected plants generally occurs within two months after symptom appearance, although in severe infections complete collapse may occur within 16 days, indicating the aggressive nature of the disease under conducive environmental conditions (Misra and Pandey, 2000b).
Disease Management:

Orchard sanitation and eradication of infected plants: Wilted trees should be uprooted and destroyed by burning, and trenches should be dug around infected tree trunks to prevent root-to-root spread of the pathogen (Mathur, 1956).
Careful handling during transplanting: Root injury should be minimized during transplanting, as wounds facilitate pathogen entry and establishment in the root system (Edward, 1960c).
Maintenance of tree vigour: Proper manuring, intercultural operations, and timely irrigation improve plant health and enhance tolerance against wilt infection (Edward, 1960c).

Soil disinfestation before planting: Planting pits may be treated with formalin, covered for about 3 days, and left for two weeks before transplanting to reduce soil-borne inoculum (Edward, 1960c). Green manuring and organic amendments: Disease incidence is markedly reduced under green manuring, and the use of organic nitrogen sources suppresses wilt development (Chattopadhyay and Bhattacharjya, 1968b). Application of organic manures, oil cakes, and lime: Incorporation of organic manures, oil cakes, and lime into soil helps in reducing wilt severity by improving soil health and suppressing pathogens (Das Gupta and Ghoshal, 1977).
Balanced nutrient management: Judicious application of nitrogen (N) and zinc (Zn) helps in checking the spread and severity of wilt disease (Suhag and Khera, 1986).
Chaubatia paste application: Application of Chaubatia paste (red lead + copper carbonate + lanolin) has been reported to provide effective wilt control (Anonymous, 1949).

Chemotherapeutic injection: Injection of 0.1% 8-Quinolinol sulphate into healthy or mildly infected trees provides protection against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. psidii and may aid partial recovery of infected plants (Jain, 1956).
Soil amendment with lime or gypsum: Soil treatment with 1.82 kg lime or gypsum per tree significantly reduced wilt incidence in field conditions (Mathur et al., 1964).

Pruning and fungicidal drenching: Severely affected trees may be regenerated by severe pruning, followed by four drenches/year of 0.2% Benlate or Bavistin, along with foliar sprays of Metasystox and zinc sulphate (Suhag, 1976).

Use of resistant rootstocks: Resistant species such as Psidium cattleianum var. lucidum and Syzygium cumini can be used as rootstocks because of graft compatibility, offering durable wilt resistance (Edward, 1961). Biological control: Antagonistic microorganisms such as Aspergillus niger strain AN17 and Penicillium citrinum have shown promising suppression of wilt pathogens (Misra et al., 2000; Prakash et al., 2002). Integrated eco-friendly management: An integrated approach involving biological control, soil amendments, intercropping, and improved cultural practices is recommended for sustainable management of guava wilt (Misra et al., 2001).

Integrated biological + chemical management: Combined application of Trichoderma harzianum with fungicides (e.g., Topsin M) and organic amendments such as wheat straw effectively reduced wilt/decline complexes (Ansar et al., 1994).
2. ANTHRACNOSE

Anthracnose is one of the important fungal diseases of guava and was first reported from Uttar Pradesh by Mehta in 1951. Subsequently, Rawal (1993) reported the disease from Karnataka. At present, it is considered a serious problem in guava-growing regions of Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, and Karnataka. The disease causes symptoms such as dieback, twig blight, wither tip, and fruit spots. A severe dieback phase associated with Gloeosporium psidii, resulting in plant death, was observed at Allahabad (Tandon and Agarwal, 1954), although similar symptoms were not noticed at Saharanpur (Tandon and Singh, 1969). Anthracnose of guava has also been recorded in several other countries including Taiwan and Southern Nigeria. Yang and Chuang (1994) reported the disease from Taiwan, while Amusa et al. (2005) documented its severe incidence in Nigeria, where about 80 per cent of guava plants were infected and over 40 per cent of the fruits showed severe anthracnose symptoms. Anthracnose of guava consists of two distinct phases, namely the die back phase and the fruit and leaf infection phase.
Fig 3: Die back of guava Fig 4: Anthracnose leaf spot of guava
DIE BACK PHASE
Symptomatology:

The die back phase is characterized by drying of tender shoots and branches from the tip backwards. Initially, the green growing tips turn dark brown and later become black due to necrosis. The infection gradually extends backwards causing drying and death of twigs and branches. Young leaves, buds, flowers, and tender shoots are highly susceptible to infection. Infected leaves droop, dry, and fall off, leaving the twigs bare. Under moist conditions, minute black acervuli appear scattered over the dead tissues. Severe infection may result in partial or complete death of the plant (Tandon and Agarwal, 1954).
Causal organism:

The die back phase of guava anthracnose is caused by a fungal pathogen known as Colletotrichum psidii Curzi. Earlier, this fungus was identified as Gloeosporium psidii Delacroix, while its sexual stage was named Glomerella psidii (Del.) Sheld. The fungus produces acervuli containing setae and conidia on infected twigs and shoots. Conidia are hyaline, unicellular, and sickle-shaped.
Disease cycle
Primary spread:

The fungus survives in infected twigs, dried branches, mummified fruits, and diseased plant debris left in the orchard. These infected materials act as the primary source of inoculum during the next season. The pathogen may also remain latent in infected buds and shoots.
Secondary spread:

During moist and rainy weather, acervuli formed on infected twigs produce abundant conidia. These spores are disseminated mainly by wind and rain splash to healthy shoots, leaves, and tender twigs, resulting in fresh infections and progressive die back symptoms.
Disease Management:
Prune and destroy infected twigs, dried shoots, and mummified fruits to reduce the source of inoculum.

Maintain proper orchard sanitation and aeration to minimize humidity and disease spread. Spray Bordeaux mixture (3:3:50) at regular intervals for effective disease reduction. Apply Perenox at 0.22 or 0.33 per cent to reduce die back symptoms and mummification of fruits (Tandon and Agarwal, 1954).
FRUIT AND LEAF INFECTION PHASE:
Symptomatology:

The fruit and leaf infection phase mainly affects fruits, leaves, flowers, and tender twigs. On unripe fruits, small pin-head sized dark brown to black spots appear, which later enlarge into circular, sunken lesions measuring about 5-6 mm in diameter. The lesions contain minute black stromata at the centre and produce creamy or pinkish spore masses under humid conditions. Several lesions coalesce to form larger infected areas. In severe cases, the affected portion becomes corky, hard, and cracked. On ripe fruits, tissue softening and fruit rot develop. Leaves show necrotic lesions on the margins or tips, while infected flowers and buds turn brown, dry, and shed prematurely. Tender twigs may also wither from the tip downwards, giving a characteristic wither-tip appearance.
Causal organism:

The fruit and leaf infection phase is also caused by Colletotrichum psidii Curzi. The fungus infects tender leaves, flowers, and fruits, producing characteristic dark, sunken lesions with black stromata and creamy or pinkish spore masses under humid conditions.
Disease cycle
Primary spread:

The pathogen persists in infected fruits, fallen leaves, dried twigs, and other diseased plant debris. Latently infected fruits and plant parts also serve as important sources of primary inoculum during the rainy season.
Secondary spread:

Conidia produced in acervuli on infected fruits, leaves, and twigs are spread by rain splash and wind to healthy fruits and foliage. Warm temperature and high relative humidity favour rapid multiplication and repeated secondary infection, especially during the rainy season crop.
Epidemiology:

Anthracnose of guava is favored by warm and humid environmental conditions. The pathogen survives on infected twigs, leaves, fruits, and plant debris, serving as primary sources of inoculum. Conidia are disseminated mainly through rain splash, wind, insects, and irrigation water. Disease development is highest at temperatures of 25-30°C and relative humidity above 90%. Prolonged rainfall and leaf wetness promote spore germination, infection, and rapid disease spread. The pathogen often establishes latent infections in immature fruits, with symptoms becoming prominent during fruit ripening and storage.
Disease Management:
Spray Bordeaux mixture (3:3:50) at 7-day intervals for effective management of anthracnose (Tandon and Singh, 1969).
Apply copper oxychloride or cuprous oxide to reduce fruit and leaf infection (Tandon and Singh, 1969).
Monthly sprays of Difolatan (0.3%) and Dithane Z-78 (0.2%) effectively control the disease (Anonymous, 1974).
Dip harvested fruits in 500 ppm tetracycline solution for 20 minutes to reduce post-harvest fruit rot (Gupta et al., 1973).
Treat fruits with sodium metabisulphite and stable bleaching powder under in vivo conditions for better disease management (Singh and Sharma, 1982).
Apply fungicides such as Thiabendazole, Aureofungin, Thiophanate methyl, and Benomyl to inhibit fungal growth and acervulus formation (Sharma et al., 1983).
Vitigram blue at 50 ppm and boric acid help in restricting acervulus formation and hyphal growth (Butt et al., 1995).
Remove and destroy infected fruits, leaves, and twigs to minimize secondary spread of the pathogen.
FRUIT CANKER

Fruit canker or scabby fruit canker of guava is an important fungal disease caused mainly by Pestalotia psidii Pat. (syn. Pestalotiopsis psidii) was recorded from Bombay (Chibber,1911) and later from Mysore (Narsimhan, 1938; Venkatakrishniah, 1952), Thane, Dharwar, Poona (Patel et al., 1950), Ponta Vally in Himachal Pradesh (Verma and Sharma, 1976) and Lucknow (Misra and Prakash, 1986). Scabby canker can drastically reduce fruit yield during the preharvest stage, and can also lead to fruit losses during postharvest storage (Kwee et al., 1990). In India, P. psidii causes postharvest damage of ripe guava fruits (Kaushik et al.,1972). It mainly affects green fruits and occasionally leaves, causing severe reduction in fruit quality and market value. Under favorable humid conditions, the disease becomes serious during both pre-harvest and post-harvest stages, resulting in malformed, mummified and prematurely dropped fruits Causal Organism:

The disease is caused primarily by Pestalotia psidii Pat. Several workers also reported association of Colletotrichum psidii Curzi and Glomerella psidii with canker symptoms, but Pestalotia psidii is considered the principal pathogen responsible for the disease (Narsimhan, 1940; Venkatakrishniah, 1952). Pestalotiopsis is characterized by spores having mostly four-euseptate and pigmented median cells with two to four apical appendages arising as tubular extensions from the apical cell and a centric basal appendage (The pathogen produces dark black pycnidia containing conidia and conidiophores. The conidia are typically five-celled, oblong to fusoid, with three pigmented median cells and hyaline terminal cells bearing apical appendages and a basal pedicel. Young mycelium is white to pinkish, septate and cottony in appearance (Patel et al., 1950).
Symptoms:

The disease occurs mainly on young green fruits and rarely on leaves. Initial symptoms appear as minute brown or rust-colored circular necrotic spots on fruits. As the disease progresses, the epidermis ruptures in a circular manner forming raised margins with depressed centers, giving a characteristic crater-like appearance. In severe infections, numerous cankerous lesions develop, causing fruits to crack open and expose seeds. Diseased fruits remain small, hard, malformed, mummified and often drop prematurely. Older lesions may show white fungal growth with abundant spores. On leaves, small rusty-brown angular spots may occasionally develop (Patel et al., 1950; Venkatakrishniah, 1952).

Disease cycle
Primary Spread:
The pathogen survives in infected fruits, diseased plant debris and mummified fruits left in orchards. Conidia present in pycnidia serve as the primary source of inoculum.
Initial infection generally occurs through wounds on young green fruits.
The fungus acts mainly as a wound parasite, entering through injuries caused by insects, abrasions or mechanical damage (Patel et al., 1950).
Secondary Spread:
Secondary spread occurs mainly through conidia dispersed by rain splash, wind and irrigation water. High humidity favors rapid sporulation and repeated infection cycles.
Infected fruits during storage and transport may also spread the pathogen to healthy fruits during post-harvest handling.
Rainy season conditions favor rapid dissemination and disease development (Verma and Sharma, 1976).
Epidemiology:

Disease development is favored by warm and humid environmental conditions. Maximum disease incidence occurs at temperatures between 25-30°C with high relative humidity (Kaushik et al., 1972). The pathogen grows vigorously between 15-30°C, with optimum growth and sporulation around 26°C. Spore germination is maximum near 30°C and does not occur below 15°C or above 40°C (Ramaswami et al., 1984). Relative humidity above 98% is essential for spore germination.

The fungus grows best on media containing sucrose, mannitol and dextrin, while optimum pH for growth ranges between 3.9 and 4.9 (Tandon, 1950). Young green fruits are highly susceptible, especially when wounded. Rainy season conditions favor rapid disease spread, whereas winter conditions promote formation of typical canker lesions.

x: Remove and destroy infected and mummified fruits.
Maintain orchard sanitation and avoid fruit injuries.
Improve aeration within orchards to reduce humidity.

blocks.x: Three to four sprays of 1% Bordeaux mixture or lime sulphur (1:25 dilution) at 15-day intervals effectively reduce disease spread (Venkatakrishniah, 1952).
Botanical Control:

Leaf extracts of Azadirachta indica and Ocimum sanctum inhibit spore germination. Treatment of fruits with Ocimum sanctum extract before or after inoculation reduces infection without affecting fruit flavor (Pandey et al., 1983).
Other Measures:
Use disease-free planting material.
Proper post-harvest handling and storage reduce fruit losses.
Integrated disease management practices combining sanitation, fungicides and botanical extracts are most effective.
4. ALGAL LEAF AND FRUIT SPOT OF GUAVA
Introduction:

Algal leaf and fruit spot of guava is caused mainly by the green alga Cephaleuros virescens. The disease produces spots on leaves and fruits, reducing photosynthetic activity, but generally does not cause severe economic losses (Ruehle, 1941). Ruehle (1941) reported the disease on leaves, fruits, twigs, and bark of guava in Florida, with severe infection mainly on leaves and fruits. Thirumalachar (1945) reported Cephaleuros parasiticus causing fruit blemishes in Mysore. Yadav (1953) later reported the disease from Bihar. Misra and Prakash (1986) observed disease incidence up to 30% in Lucknow and Sitapur districts of Uttar Pradesh.
Fig 7: Algal leaf spot on leaf Fig 8: Algal leaf spot on Fruit
Symptomatology
On Leaves

The disease primarily infects immature leaves during the early spring flush. Initial symptoms appear as minute, shallow brown lesions which gradually enlarge to about 23 mm in diameter. Spots may vary from tiny specks to large irregular patches and may occur scattered or densely crowded. Infection is commonly seen near leaf tips, margins, and midrib regions. In guava, lesions often extend through the entire leaf lamina, and sporulation generally occurs on the abaxial (lower) surface of leaves (Ruehle, 1941; Marlatt and Campbell, 1980a,b).
On Fruits

Immature fruits develop dark black lesions. As fruits enlarge, infected areas become sunken and cracks frequently develop on older lesions. Infection remains superficial, affecting only a few cell layers beneath the epidermis. Fruit lesions are usually smaller than leaf lesions and vary from dark green to brown or black (Ruehle, 1941; Marlatt and Campbell, 1980a,b).
Time of Infection

Symptoms generally appear during April and disease severity increases from May to August. Heavy rainfall from July to September favours abundant sporulation, resulting in maximum disease incidence during September.
The disease is rarely observed during October and symptoms are generally absent during winter (Ruehle, 1941; Marlatt and Campbell, 1980a,b).
Causal Organism

The disease is mainly caused by Cephaleuros virescens [syn. C. mycoidea] (Ruehle, 1941). Thirumalachar (1945) attributed the disease to Cephaleuros parasiticus, while Yadav (1953) and Marlatt and Campbell (1980a,b) also reported Cephaleuros spp. associated with the disease. The pathogen develops between the cuticle and epidermis of host tissue, penetrates epidermal cells, and causes cell death. The disease is commonly called “red rust” because the upper surface of the thallus bears erects yellow to reddish reproductive structures.
Epidemiology

Algal leaf spot of guava is caused by the green alga Cephaleuros virescens and is prevalent in warm, humid, and high-rainfall regions. The pathogen survives on infected leaves and twigs and produces sporangia that serve as the primary source of inoculum. Disease development is favored by temperatures of 25-30°C, relative humidity above 90%, and prolonged periods of leaf wetness. Sporangia are dispersed mainly by wind-driven rain and irrigation water. Dense orchard canopies, poor air circulation, and shaded conditions increase disease severity. The disease is most severe during the rainy season when moisture availability promotes algal growth and infection.
Morphological Characters
The thallus consists of flat, short, densely crowded branched filaments with irregularly branched rhizoids beneath.

Fruiting structures bear upright multicellular filaments with 1-8 sharply curved pedicels. Each pedicel carries a pear-shaped to spherical sporangium containing about 8-32 biflagellate motile spores (Marlatt and Campbell, 1980a).
Special Features in Guava
A distinct thallus is generally absent on the upper leaf surface.
Lesions rapidly spread through the entire leaf lamina and sporulation mainly occurs on the lower surface of infected leaves.
Heavy rainfall greatly enhances sporulation (Marlatt and Campbell, 1980a,b).
Changes in Physiology:
Changes in Carbohydrates

Glucose and sucrose contents decrease in infected tissues, whereas fructose content increases. Cellulose and pectin contents increase, while lignin content remains unaffected (Vidyasekaran and Parambaramani, 1971b).
Changes in Nitrogen and Proteins
Total protein content decreases along with ammonical, nitrite, amino, and amide nitrogen levels (Vidyasekaran and Parambaramani, 1971a).
Changes in Amino Acids
Glutamic acid and alanine increase considerably.
Glycine decreases sharply, while valine remains unchanged (Vidyasekaran and Parambaramani, 1971a).
Changes in Water Relations and Minerals
Transpiration rate increases and leaf water content decreases.
Potassium and phosphorus contents decline, whereas sodium accumulates in infected tissues. Magnesium shows slight increase while sulphur decreases.
Iron and manganese accumulate, whereas copper content decreases (Vidyasekaran and Parambaramani, 1972)
Control Measures

Spray copper oxychloride at 0.3% concentration for 3-4 times at 15-day intervals. Sprays during the rainy season are more effective in controlling the disease (Ruehle, 1941). Biological control using an ascomycetous parasite resembling Strigula astridiza on Cephaleuros parasiticus has also been suggested (Thirumalachar, 1945).Top of Form
